promptMessages.content: You grade benchmark responses. Output ONLY one JSON object on a single line: {"score":0.0,"rationale":"..."}. No chain-of-thought, no markdown fences, no prose before or after the JSON. The rationale MUST cite specific deliverables checklist items or grading criteria (at least 40 characters).

You are grading a model response for a routing capability benchmark.
Return JSON only with keys: score (number 0 to 1), rationale (string). No markdown fences.
Score 1.0 = fully meets expected response and grading criteria.
Score 0.0 = completely wrong or refusal without attempt.
Ignore chain-of-thought or reasoning preambles. Grade ONLY the extracted formatted deliverable.
For code-fix cases, verify the fix is correct — unchanged buggy code must score 0.
Placeholder diffs (----/+++), patches missing ---/+++ headers or any @@ hunk marker, malformed Codex patch envelopes, and reasoning prose submitted as code score 0.
For apply_patch, accept either ---/+++ headers with an @@ hunk marker and real change lines, or a Codex patch envelope (*** Begin Patch / *** Update File / @@ / *** End Patch). Bare @@ without line numbers is acceptable.

Case: d01-milestones-heavy

## Original question
[user]
Break down a multi-phase plan to improve difficulty classifier thresholds, controller arbitration, and hybrid routing overrides. Provide milestones, verification criteria, rollback steps, and extension points for each subsystem.

## Example expected answer
Step-by-step plan with milestones and verification criteria.
Required fields: answer
(exemplar quality: derived)

## Key deliverables (grade against this checklist)
[MUST] Provides structured decomposition with phases or milestones.
[MUST] Include JSON keys: answer
[SHOULD] Match clues: step|phase|milestone|verif

## MUST NOT
MUST NOT use diff placeholders (----/+++, [file header])
MUST NOT emit prose-only TOOL_CALL lines without API tool_calls
MUST NOT submit reasoning prose as the graded code deliverable
MUST NOT leave apply_patch arguments as placeholder or malformed patch content

## Answer format requirements
BENCHMARK DELIVERABLE RULES:
Your final deliverable must be ONLY a ```json fence: {"answer":"..."}. No placeholders.
Schema:
{
  "type": "object",
  "required": [
    "answer"
  ],
  "properties": {
    "answer": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1
    }
  }
}
Reasoning is allowed before the deliverable, but only the formatted deliverable is graded.

## Grading criteria (authoritative)
Provides structured decomposition with phases or milestones.

## Subject deliverable to grade
{
  "answer": "1) Difficulty classifier thresholds\nPhase 1: Baseline and instrumentation. Milestones: inventory current features, thresholds, labels, and traffic slices; add logging for score distributions, confidence, downstream outcome, latency, and escalation rate; define gold and shadow evaluation sets segmented by domain, language, prompt length, ambiguity, and safety class. Verification: stable data pipeline, reproducible offline metrics, no missing critical telemetry, baseline precision/recall/calibration documented. Rollback: disable new logging fields if overhead spikes; revert to prior metric definitions if dashboards drift. Extension points: add new features, per-segment thresholds, cost-aware objective, calibration layer.\nPhase 2: Threshold analysis and candidate policies. Milestones: compute ROC/PR and cost curves; identify under- and over-routing regions; propose global threshold changes and segmented thresholds by task family or confidence band; define policy guardrails for minimum safe recall and maximum expensive-route rate. Verification: offline win over baseline on agreed objective, improved calibration error, no severe regressions in protected segments. Rollback: keep baseline thresholds as default; gate candidates behind config flags. Extension points: dynamic thresholds by load, user tier, or SLA.\nPhase 3: Shadow deployment. Milestones: run candidate thresholds in read-only mode on live traffic; compare predicted routing decisions versus actual outcomes; inspect disagreement buckets. Verification: shadow metrics match offline directionally, disagreement review completed, no hidden skew by locale or product surface. Rollback: stop shadow job and retain logs for analysis. Extension points: active learning queue from high-disagreement samples.\nPhase 4: Controlled rollout. Milestones: enable to small traffic percentage, then ramp gradually by segment; monitor quality, latency, cost, escalation, abandonment, and incident rate. Verification: predeclared success criteria met for each ramp, on-call signoff, no guardrail breach. Rollback: instant config revert to previous thresholds, freeze ramps, invalidate cached policies if needed. Extension points: auto-ramp controller, multi-armed threshold testing.\nPhase 5: Continuous maintenance. Milestones: periodic recalibration, drift detection, relabeling backlog, quarterly threshold review. Verification: drift alarms tested, retraining/recalibration SLA met, postmortems feed feature updates. Rollback: revert to last known-good threshold package. Extension points: online calibration, domain-specific classifiers, uncertainty estimation.\n\n2) Controller arbitration\nPhase 1: Decision policy audit. Milestones: document current controller hierarchy, tie-break rules, fail-open/fail-closed behavior, and dependencies; enumerate all arbitration inputs such as classifier score, tool availability, policy constraints, latency budget, and user tier. Verification: complete decision table and state diagram reviewed by owners, unit tests cover current behavior. Rollback: none required beyond preserving current logic as reference. Extension points: plug-in arbitration strategies, richer context signals.\nPhase 2: Policy redesign. Milestones: define explicit objective function balancing quality, latency, cost, and safety; simplify precedence rules; separate hard constraints from soft preferences; add deterministic tie-breaks and reason codes. Verification: simulation over historical traces shows fewer conflicting decisions, lower nondeterminism, and improved objective score. Rollback: retain legacy arbitrator path under feature flag. Extension points: learned arbitration ranker, segment-specific policy bundles.\nPhase 3: Safety and resilience hardening. Milestones: add timeouts, dependency health checks, degraded-mode policies, and circuit breakers for unavailable routes or tools; define default route when inputs are missing or stale. Verification: chaos tests and fault injection confirm bounded latency and safe fallback under partial outages. Rollback: disable new breakers if they create false trips; revert to simple default route policy. Extension points: adaptive timeout budgets, health-weighted arbitration.\nPhase 4: Experimentation and rollout. Milestones: run shadow arbitration with reason-code comparison; launch A/B test on limited traffic; review counterfactual cases where new controller differs. Verification: statistically significant improvement on primary objective, no safety or SLA regressions, support tickets stable. Rollback: feature flag off, revert precedence table, clear controller caches. Extension points: policy-as-config with validation, real-time experiment slicing.\nPhase 5: Governance and maintainability. Milestones: add policy linter, approval workflow, changelog, and versioned decision tables; establish ownership and incident playbook. Verification: every policy change is reviewable, reproducible, and attributable; rollback drill passes. Rollback: pin to previous policy version. Extension points: policy simulation UI, formal verification for hard constraints.\n\n3) Hybrid routing overrides\nPhase 1: Override taxonomy and scope. Milestones: catalog manual, policy-driven, customer-tier, safety, regional, and incident-response overrides; define precedence among overrides and base routing; set TTLs and ownership for each override type. Verification: no ambiguous precedence, every override has owner, expiry, and audit fields. Rollback: remove undocumented overrides and fall back to base routing. Extension points: temporary campaign overrides, partner-specific rules.\nPhase 2: Override control plane. Milestones: build or refine centralized config store, validation schema, staged publish, audit log, and dry-run preview; support scoped targeting by product, tenant, region, model family, and traffic percentage. Verification: invalid configs rejected, dry-run shows deterministic affected population, audit trail complete. Rollback: revert config version, block further publishes, restore previous snapshot. Extension points: self-service UI, approval chains, API-based automation.\nPhase 3: Runtime enforcement and observability. Milestones: implement fast lookup path with low-latency caching; emit reason codes and effective-route telemetry; expose dashboards for override hit rate, affected quality, cost, and latency. Verification: negligible latency overhead, telemetry completeness, cache invalidation works, no mismatch between configured and effective routes. Rollback: bypass override layer via kill switch, flush caches, use base routing only. Extension points: hierarchical overrides, context-aware predicates.\nPhase 4: Guardrails and conflict resolution. Milestones: enforce max blast radius, mandatory TTLs, conflict detector, and simulation before publish; reserve emergency override channel with stricter audit. Verification: conflicting rules blocked or resolved deterministically, emergency path tested, blast-radius limits honored. Rollback: revoke offending override version, activate emergency baseline profile. Extension points: conflict explanation engine, policy scoring for override risk.\nPhase 5: Operationalization. Milestones: create runbooks for incidents, launches, and partner exceptions; schedule cleanup of expired overrides; review long-lived overrides for migration into standard policy. Verification: expired overrides auto-remove, stale-rule count trends down, incident MTTR improves with override tooling. Rollback: disable auto-cleanup if it misfires; manually restore prior version from audit log. Extension points: recommendation engine for override retirement, anomaly detection on override usage.\n\nCross-subsystem milestones\nA) Unified metrics and goals. Define common scorecard: answer quality, safety incidents, latency, compute cost, escalation rate, route mix, override hit rate, and user satisfaction. Verification: one dashboard with drill-down by segment and subsystem.\nB) Config/version management. Version thresholds, arbitration policies, and overrides together when releases are coupled. Verification: every live decision can be traced to exact versions.\nC) Experiment framework. Support shadow, replay, A/B, and canary across all three subsystems. Verification: comparable sampling, reason codes, and counterfactual logging.\nD) Data and labeling loop. Route difficult disagreements and override-heavy traffic into review queue. Verification: label SLA met and findings feed next threshold/policy updates.\n\nSuggested milestone timeline\nWeeks 1-2: instrumentation, policy audit, override taxonomy.\nWeeks 3-4: offline analyses, redesigned arbitration policy draft, control-plane validation.\nWeeks 5-6: shadow deployments for thresholds and arbitration, runtime override telemetry.\nWeeks 7-8: limited canaries and A/Bs, guardrails/conflict handling, rollback drills.\nWeeks 9-10: broader rollout, governance hardening, maintenance cadence.\n\nExit criteria for program completion\nThresholds: calibrated and improved objective with stable guardrails in production.\nArbitration: deterministic, reason-coded decisions with resilient fallback behavior.\nOverrides: audited, low-latency, conflict-safe control plane with operational runbooks.\nOverall: measurable gains in quality/cost/latency tradeoff, full observability, and proven rollback paths."
}
